## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Babbujātaka* (Ja 137) is a short narrative text preserved in the *Jātaka* collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [Fausböll 1877]. Set at Jetavana, the Buddha recounts the story in connection with the monastic rule concerning Kāṇā's mother (*Kāṇamātāsikkhāpada*) [Fausböll 1877; Horner]. According to the frame narrative, the lay follower Kāṇā was divorced by her husband after four monks successively accepted the cakes she had prepared to take home; the Buddha explains to the assembled monks that this was not the first time those same individuals had caused distress to Kāṇā [Burlingame 1921; Heim 2014; Horner].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta was born as a stone- or gem-cutter (*pāsāṇakoṭṭakamaṇikāra*) [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877]. A mouse, who was Kāṇā in that lifetime, lived in a crystal cavity and was systematically harassed by four cats (*babbu*, glossed by the commentary as *bilāra*) demanding meat and food [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877; Horner]. The single canonical verse (*gāthā*) highlights this predicament: "Where one cat is found, there a second appears, and a third, and a fourth; this is your hole, o cats" (*Yatth' eko labhate babbu...*) [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877]. In the identification of characters (*samodhāna*), the four cats are identified as the four monks, the mouse as Kāṇā (or Kāṇā's mother), and the stone-cutter as the Buddha [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877; Horner]. This narrative is also related in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and referenced in Vinaya commentary traditions [Burlingame 1921; Heim 2014; Horner].
